messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two years old when he was mugged outside a subway station in the financial district where he had ducked in to use the bathroom before his evening commute home. Two men approached from behind a column—he had not seen them until they were already moving toward him. One grabbed his arm while the other shoved him against the tiled wall. The impact knocked the wind from his lungs. They took his wallet, his phone, his watch. What stayed with him most vividly was not the force of the shove but the smell of stale cigarette smoke mixed with something chemical, and the taste of blood from where his lip split against his teeth. One of the men had leaned close to his ear and said something low and fast that Marcus could not fully process in the moment. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. A transit officer found him sitting on the floor a few minutes later, shaking. Now, at thirty-eight, Marcus has spent six years trying to rebuild a life that appears, from the outside, largely intact. He married Sarah three years ago. He teaches high school history at a public school in a stable neighborhood. He maintains friendships, pays his mortgage, shows up to faculty meetings. But the texture of his daily existence has become increasingly constrained, and in the past year the constraints have begun to visibly affect his work and his marriage.

Marcus has come to understand the world as fundamentally unpredictable and hostile in ways he cannot quite articulate to others. Faces have become a source of constant vigilance. When he stands before his class—a room of teenagers he intellectually knows pose no threat—his eyes move across their expressions searching for signs of aggression, calculation, the micro-expressions he has convinced himself reveal true intent. He finds himself studying the set of a student's jaw, the intensity of their gaze, wondering if something dangerous is being concealed. This hypervigilance has exhausted him. Colleagues have noticed that he seems tense, that he sometimes appears startled by ordinary classroom sounds—a door slamming, a desk scraping—and recoils as if struck. One student asked, in the direct way teenagers do, why he always looked scared. The startle responses are involuntary; his body responds to sudden noise as though threat is imminent, his nervous system unable to distinguish between the harmless scrape of furniture and the dangerous approach of the men from six years ago.

Crowded spaces have become nearly intolerable. The subway is out of the question; Marcus drives to school now, though driving itself has become complicated. He cannot tolerate passengers. When Sarah suggests they take a trip together, or when a colleague asks for a ride to a conference, Marcus finds himself inventing reasons why this is impossible. Last month, when Sarah's sister visited from out of state and needed a ride from the airport, Marcus's anxiety was so acute that he had to pull over twice. Sarah had to take over driving. The silence in the car afterward felt accusatory, though she said nothing. He knows she does not understand why he cannot simply manage this, why he cannot sit in a car with another person without his heart rate climbing and his palms becoming slick. Movie theaters are impossible. Shopping malls are impossible. The crowded hallways between classes at school have become a gauntlet he dreads. He times his movement through them carefully, positioning himself against walls, always aware of where the nearest exit is located. The moment he enters any enclosed space—a classroom, a staff room, a restaurant—his attention fractures. Part of him is present in conversation; another part is mapping the room's geometry, identifying windows, doors, alternative routes. He is exhausted by this constant spatial calculation, yet the moment he stops doing it, panic rises.

The memories themselves come without warning and with a sensory completeness that unmoors him from the present. He will be standing at the front of his classroom explaining the causes of the Civil War, and suddenly he tastes blood again, smells that chemical smoke, feels the impact of the wall against his spine. The memory does not feel like remembering—it feels like the event is happening now, all of it at once, pressing in from every direction. These episodes last seconds or minutes, but they leave him shaken, disoriented. His students have learned not to ask questions when he goes quiet mid-sentence. What troubles Marcus most deeply is the conviction that this happened because the world is simply dangerous, that he was unlucky, and that no real justice has been possible. The police never found the men. The case went nowhere. He has come to believe that institutions—the police, the legal system—fundamentally failed him, and that this failure is not exceptional but revealing. It showed him something true about how the world actually works. This belief sits beneath everything else, a bedrock conviction that shapes how he moves through his days. Sarah suggested, gently and then less gently, that he see someone. She said she loved him but that she was frightened by how much space the fear was taking up in their life together. Marcus finally called a therapist last week. He is afraid of what it will mean if the fear cannot be fixed, and hopeful, in a way he has not allowed himself to be in years, that someone might help him understand why his mind has decided the world is a place where he cannot be safe.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Taste Vividness: The vignette describes Marcus tasting blood during intrusive memories ('he tastes blood again'), but this is presented as part of the full sensory reliving of the event itself. The patient's reported symptom 'Taste Vividness' specifically refers to tasting what was tasted during the event when the memory returns—implying taste as a distinct, isolated sensory trigger or component that recurs independently. While blood is mentioned, the vignette does not clearly isolate taste as a specific, vivid sensory element that returns separately or distinctly from the full sensory experience. The core distinction is that the symptom suggests taste functions as a particular sensory anchor, whereas the vignette subsumes it entirely within the 'Full Sensory Reliving' description.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
